title: Bad Education
full_review:
A young film director looking for his next project. A struggling actor with sultry good looks and a shrouded past. A predatory priest. These are the spicy ingredients in "Bad Education" (Sony Classics), the newest decadent dish served up by Spanish filmmaker Pedro Almodovar.

For Almodovar, the controversial film -- chosen as the opening-night selection of the 2004 Cannes Film Festival and the centerpiece of the 2004 New York Film Festival -- continues his trend toward more serious-toned material (including 1999's "All About My Mother" and 2001's "Talk to Her") and away from the ribald comedies which won him international acclaim, like "Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown" (1988) and "Tie Me Up, Tie Me Down!" (1989).

Still, while the movie deals with the hot-button issues of priest pedophilia and homosexuality, the Iberian auteur manages to sprinkle in some of his trademark humor in exploring his
touchstone themes of sin, seduction and cinema.

Heavily influenced by film-noir classics and tenuously inspired by personal recollections, the picture's story-within-a-story framework covers three time periods in Spain: 1964, 1977 and 1980, where most of the action takes place.

Revisiting themes explored in his "Law of Desire" (1986), Almodovar opens his new film in Madrid in 1980, where Enrique Goded (Fele Martinez), a successful movie director, is combing through newspaper stories searching for script ideas. An attractive young man (Gael Garcia Bernal) serendipitously shows up at the production office and introduces himself as Ignacio, an old classmate with whom Enrique had been enamored while they were students at a strict Catholic boarding school.

Ignacio gives Enrique a semiautobiographical short story he wrote about their youthful experiences, in particular, the pederast predations of Father Manolo (Daniel Gimenez-Cacho), the school's headmaster, whose lustful fixation for Ignacio cut short the budding boyhood romance. In the fictional version, Enrique grows up to be a frustrated family man, while Ignacio headlines a flamboyant drag-queen cabaret act.

Enrique agrees to turn it into a film and casts Ignacio in the lead role.

The plot shuttles back and forth, not only between past and present, but between the "real" world and the multilayered memories of the short story, weaving a triangular tapestry of deception, blackmail and murder created by the intersection of the three men's lives.

The concentric story lines are fuzzy at times, making it difficult to sort out reality from fiction within the world of the film. Keeping track of who's who also requires some heavy mental lifting -- or at least a scorecard -- for some actors perform multiple roles, or, as in the case of Father Manolo, the same character is played by two different actors (Gimenez-Cacho and, later, Lluis Homar). However, Almodovar, at the top of his cinematic game, manages to keep all the balls in the air without dropping any.

"Bad Education" contains several homoerotic scenes which are extremely suggestive without being necessarily explicit. In fact, the only nudity is a fleeting shot of Enrique's rump after he emerges from a skinny-dipping game of cat-and-mouse with Ignacio in his pool.

Despite charges to the contrary, Almodovar -- an agnostic who was raised Catholic -- has publicly stated that it was not his intention to make an anti-clerical film. Still, such denials must be weighed against what actually appears on screen. On this count, the verdict could go either way. The very choice of setting the story in a Catholic school is telling, as are the sinister shades with which he paints the two main priests, Father Manolo and Father Jose (Francisco Maestre) -- a sexual predator and a bullying brute, respectively.

However, while such unflattering portraits of ecclesiastical authority are hardly accidental, Almodovar's primary motive seems to have been to use Father Manolo's abuse of power as a catalyst for the story rather than as a weapon to target the church in general for condemnation. The film does take some shots at Catholicism and includes an irreverent scene where two characters
steal sacred vessels from a chapel.

On the positive side, by dramatizing the devastating effects sexual abuse has on victims' lives, the film can hopefully -- at least according to Sacred Heart Father Peter Malone, an Australian priest who is president of the World Catholic Association for Cinema -- "contribute to the church's continuing examination of conscience." In that sense, even a "Bad Education" can offer an opportunity for learning.

Subtitles.

Due to several intense homosexual encounters, implied pedophilia, murder without consequence, recurring drug content, transvestism, a scene of two boys masturbating, brief nudity, fleeting violence, instances of irreverent humor and frequent rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
